paragraphs.notes: B03-01 ‘they all made an excellent dinner’ → ‘they all had an excellent dinner’: real false friend. ‘Make dinner’ now means cook it, which contradicts the carvers having just served the roast; Butler's idiom means ate. ‘had’ is the plainest verb for that sense, and the edition already drops the same Butler idiom elsewhere (13 ¶2 ‘enjoyed an excellent feast’, 14 ¶25 ‘after a hearty supper’). Collision check: the new ‘had’ stands beside Butler's ‘had had enough to eat and drink’, but it is the same verb in the same sense (to eat or drink), so nothing is merged and nothing misleads; the ‘had … had had’ sequence is a mild sound echo only. Conventions intact. The only BEFORE→AFTER difference is this word.

B03-02 ‘by the treachery of Aegisthus and his wife’ → ‘by the treachery of Aegisthus and of his own wife’: real misreading, since ‘his’ binds to the nearest name, Aegisthus. Butler's ‘his’ renders Homer's reflexive ἧς ἀλόχοιο (3.235), ‘his own wife’, Agamemnon's. ‘own’ adds no content. It is the minimal disambiguator of Butler's pronoun toward his intended antecedent, and the betrayal-by-one's-own-wife reading is the one it forces. The second ‘of’ mirrors the Greek's two genitives under δόλῳ and breaks up ‘Aegisthus and his wife’ as a couple. It does not change meaning. Collision: Butler's paragraph has ‘own’ once (‘my own house’) in the same emphatic-possessive sense, so the echo reinforces rather than misleads. The residual parse ‘Aegisthus's own wife’ is grammatically possible but pragmatically implausible, so the problem is fixed. Grammar and quotation structure intact.

B03-03 ‘Here he divided his fleet’ → ‘Here Zeus divided his fleet’: real hidden-agent problem. In Butler the pronoun follows ‘Jove … made it blow hard’, and Homer's subject of διατμήξας … ἐπέλασσεν (3.291) is Zeus. Reading ‘he’ as Menelaus contradicts the narrative, since Menelaus is carried to Egypt with the other five ships, not to Crete. Naming the referent adds nothing Butler does not mean, and ‘his fleet’ can now only be Menelaus's. The name is in its Greek form per the mapping. B03-04 ‘much gold and substance’ → ‘much gold and wealth’: dead sense (‘substance’ = property; it now reads as material or drugs). ‘wealth’ is the edition's established rendering of Butler's ‘substance’ in this sense (11 ¶7, 13 ¶33, 22 ¶3, 22 ¶36, 24 ¶31; 11 ¶34 rightly keeps ‘substance’ where it means bodily substance). It does not merge with Butler's ‘treasure’ at the end of the paragraph, which stays distinct. B03-L1 ‘among people of an alien speech’ → ‘among people who spoke a foreign tongue’: I side with the lead over the adjudicator's keep. The phrase carries the dead count-noun ‘a speech’ (= a language), which now reads as an oration, and ‘alien’ has an extraterrestrial pull. ‘foreign tongue’ is Butler's own rendering of the same Greek word ἀλλόθροος at 1.183 (1 ¶13 ‘men of a foreign tongue’, kept verbatim in the edition), so the repair restores Butler's wording (D29). Butler's paragraph has no ‘spoke’, ‘foreign’ or ‘tongue’, so there is no collision. Optional alignment, not a defect: ‘among people of a foreign tongue’ would mirror 1 ¶13 exactly and keep Butler's ‘of’ construction; the AFTER is equally faithful. The unclosed quotation is correct because Nestor's speech continues into ¶24. The following are pre-existing in the accepted BEFORE, outside this change set, and not counted: ‘Zeus decreed evil’ for Butler's ‘counselled evil’ (Homer ἐφράσατο, devised); ‘the coast is more sheltered, for a small headland can make a great shelter’ echoes where Butler has ‘protected … shelter’ (harmless); and Butler's own ‘Sunium, which is the point of Athens’, where ‘point’ means headland but could be read as ‘purpose’ (a possible follow-up).
